sections.html:
Williamson County's seat is Franklin, a Harpeth River city around 21 miles below Nashville. July 2025 put the population at 90,226, a gain of 8.0 percent on the 83,454 residents of 2020. Only six Tennessee cities are larger.

Prices are steep. A typical owner-occupied house is worth $705,400 in the 2020 to 2024 figures, against a national median of $332,700. Among 33,998 households, 63.8 percent are owners. Owners paying a mortgage spend $2,542 a month at the median; owners with no loan spend $712; renters spend $1,923. The median household earns $119,528.

With values this high, small gaps between offers add up fast, so read each contract line by line. Expect buyers who weigh a big purchase carefully, so organized paperwork and a clean title help. Interstate 65 grazes the eastern side and the Mack Hatcher bypass wraps the commercial core. Five historic districts hold National Register listings, and older neighborhoods fall under local protection rules. If your place is close to the square, a quick call to City Hall before any exterior repair will tell you which rules apply.

A city levy of $0.296 applies to each $100 of assessed value, and nothing in the 2026-27 budget proposal changes it. That figure splits into a $0.2310 base rate for operations and debt and $0.0650 that came in after the latest reappraisal to pay for infrastructure and city services. The city itself calls the rate one of Tennessee's lowest. Assessed values are redone every four years.

Owners receive just one statement. County, Franklin Special School District and city taxes all travel together through the Williamson County Trustee. To learn what a given parcel owes, ring 615-790-5709. For assessed value or a changed billing address, the assessor answers at 615-790-5708.

Waiving, prorating or releasing tax or interest is outside the trustee's power. The person who owns the house on January 1 is the name on that year's bill, so anyone selling mid-year passes the cost to the buyer through the closing statement.

Dates repeat annually, and anything paid before March carries no interest.

Williamson County tax bill calendar
DateWhat happens
Early OctoberStatements go out by mail
First Monday of OctoberPayment window opens
End of FebruaryFinal day to pay with no interest
March 1Interest of 1.5 percent begins and is added again on the first of each following month

Listing in autumn means the buyer's side will ask if the current bill is paid. Find your statement now. If it never came, mention that at the start so the closing agent can look the parcel up.

sections.h2: School zones, utilities and monthly fees
sections.html:
Across most of the city, Franklin Special School District covers kindergarten to eighth grade and Williamson County Schools cover high school. A few outlying areas belong to the county district from start to finish. Households often begin a search at the boundary map, so learn which district your address falls in. Private choices nearby include Battle Ground Academy, Franklin Classical School, Franklin Christian Academy, Montessori School of Franklin, New Hope Academy and Thales Academy.

Monthly costs are the next question. The city plans to lift residential trash and recycling by $1, to $34 a month, in fiscal 2027, and stormwater charges are projected to add about $20.70 a year to most bills. Water and sewer rates went up 6 percent and 5.7 percent on January 1, 2026.

Most residents get water from the city. Pockets are served by the Mallory Valley, Milcrofton and HB&TS utility districts. Middle Tennessee Electric supplies TVA power and Atmos Energy supplies gas. Confirm the providers for your street before a buyer wonders.

Franklin deeds are recorded by the Williamson County Register of Deeds, 1320 West Main Street, Suite 201, Monday to Friday 8 to 4:30. The office offers electronic filing and a fee calculator. Phone 615-790-5706.

Recording brings two state charges. Transfer tax runs 37 cents on each $100 of price. Mortgage tax is 11.5 cents on each $100 of a buyer's loan past the first $2,000. Both are collected by the register and passed to the state.

sections.h2: What happens after you accept an offer
sections.html:
After both sides sign, a title company runs the paper trail. Its staff confirm who holds title, ask your lender for the remaining loan balance, look for liens and write up the deed. Under Tennessee practice the buyer, as grantee, owes the transfer tax, while the sales contract settles every other split.

  • Find your newest tax statement and your lender's phone number before you answer an offer.
  • Request three answers from the title company ahead of closing: loan payoff, tax balance, recording plan.
  • The trustee will not prorate, so the January 1 owner rule decides who carries what.
  • You sign the deed and the title company takes it to the register.

Paying cash shortens the calendar. Without a bank there is no loan approval and no lender appraisal, which is where financed deals tend to stall. Title still has to be clear, so the list above applies to cash buyers as well.

A house in rough shape gets a cash offer with the repair cost already subtracted. That spares you staging, open houses and the repair demands after an inspection. Compare offers by what you keep after repairs and carrying costs.

Start a folder with your purchase papers, the latest tax statement and permit records for any work you paid for. Historic district owners should add City Hall's approvals for past exterior changes, which a buyer's agent may request.

Then choose how to sell. A listing exposes the house to the most buyers, useful at these prices. Going alone keeps the commission but leaves contract and scheduling work with you. A cash sale accepts a lower price for speed and a date you can rely on. Every route ends at the same register and the same trustee.

Ask your title company which papers it wants first, and send them as one package so nothing is requested twice. Keep copies of everything you sign, including the settlement statement, because it shows how the tax bill was divided.

Selling does not erase a Franklin tax balance. Interest starts March 1 and is added monthly, so a forgotten bill keeps growing. If you owe, ask the trustee for the payoff before choosing a closing date and let the title company pay it from your proceeds. The trustee cannot reduce the charge, so getting the figure early prevents a shock on the settlement statement.

Cash buyers can still close quickly when taxes are owed, since the payoff is taken out of the price. Raise the debt on your first call.

faqs.q: How many people live in Franklin?
faqs.a: About 90,226 as of July 2025, up from 83,454 in 2020. Only six Tennessee cities are bigger.

faqs.q: What is Franklin's city property tax rate?
faqs.a: The levy is $0.296 per $100 of assessed value, and the 2026-27 budget proposal leaves it alone. County and school district charges arrive on the same bill.

faqs.q: When are Williamson County property taxes due?
faqs.a: Payment opens the first Monday of October and stays open until the end of February. From March 1, interest of 1.5 percent applies and repeats monthly.

faqs.q: Who pays Tennessee's transfer tax on a Franklin sale?
faqs.a: The buyer pays it, as grantee on the deed. The rate is 37 cents per $100 of price, and the register collects it at filing.

faqs.q: Which office records a deed for a Franklin house?
faqs.a: Williamson County Register of Deeds, Suite 201 at 1320 West Main Street. Call 615-790-5706 with fee questions.
